asr.full_text: It can be tough to get a hold of a real live person at some big name companies, now scammers are taking advantage of that. Tech support schemes are one of the newest cons the feds are cracking down on. Consumer specialist Rick Romero shows you how they work and how to protect yourself. Their Facebook page is colorful, inspirational and popular too, with more than 170,000 followers. And apparently vulnerable to hackers, who'd rescue their page from the hackers and keep them out. They also were supposedly putting on some kind of device so that we couldn't be hacked again. Turns out Teresa wasn't talking to Facebook. In fact, the social networking giant doesn't even offer phone tech support. Facebook says this was undoubtedly a scam. And the feds say they've received thousands of complaints about similar tech support scams. The goal is to get consumers to pay hundreds of dollars for unnecessary computer repair services. The Federal Trade Commission recently launched a major tech support scam, Crackdown, filing complaints against several companies based mostly in India. I can just help you out, only if you allow me to get into your computer, Ma'am. Ma'am, we are a two-person company, OK? Could you just roll-call on Facebook? I never expected that I wasn't speaking to Facebook because they answered the phone call with This Is Facebook Technical Support So, don't use online search results to find a company's tech support number instead, go to the company's website directly and look for that contact information. Never give control of your computer to a third party that you're unsure about. And if someone calls you claiming you have a computer problem, hang up. This is Rick Romero, ABC 7 Eyewitness News.

annotation.contextual_rationale: This video is non-scam content because it presents a consumer-news investigation explaining reported callers who claimed to be Facebook technical support and requested computer access. The report uses cautionary framing, states that Facebook does not offer phone technical support, and advises viewers how to verify support contacts and protect computer access. Although an invoice-like screen shows USD 129 for computer maintenance, the available video evidence does not connect it to a viewer-directed offer by the news segment.
annotation.fine_grained_rationale: The primary content is an investigation and warning: it explains reported tech-support schemes, describes the reported Facebook-support identity claim and computer-access request, and provides protective advice rather than promoting participation.
